title: Air purifier: safe teardown
summary: Take the HEPA and carbon filters, the fan and motor, the control board and any dust or odour sensors. Some units also hold a UV-C lamp, which contains mercury and harms eyes and skin if it is ever lit in the open, or an ionizer with a high-voltage section. Unplug first, and handle used filters outdoors: they hold what they caught.

steps.text: Unplug it and keep the plug where you can see it, and don't touch the lamp or open the case until it has been unplugged for 5 minutes. Read the labels and buttons: a UV or UV-C button, or a 'lamp contains mercury' notice, means a UV-C lamp inside; an Ion, Ionizer or PlasmaWave button means a high-voltage section.
Take it outdoors or to an airy spot, open the filter cover and lift out the filters. Put each used filter straight into a bag and tie it.
steps.warn: A used filter holds what it caught: dust, pollen, mould spores, microbes and smoke. Wear a dust mask (P2 or N95) and gloves, and don't shake or blow it out indoors.

steps.text: UV-C models: find the lamp. On the GermGuardian AC4825 it sits under the filter behind a metal shield held by two screws. Take off the shield, wear gloves and safety glasses, hold the bulb in a cloth and pull it straight out (some types twist a quarter turn first). Wrap it and keep it in a rigid box.
steps.warn: The lamp holds mercury. If it breaks: everyone out, air the room at least 15 minutes, no vacuum or broom. Scoop with stiff card, lift the rest with sticky tape, seal it all in a jar. Never power the unit with a lamp shield or cover off.

steps.text: Wait until it has been unplugged at least 5 minutes. Look for the case screws under the filter, the feet and any labels, and undo them. Then work round the seam with a plastic pry tool to release the clips, and lift the shell off.
steps.warn: Don't touch anything inside yet: the power board's capacitor may still be charged.

steps.text: Find the power board: the one the mains cord connects to. Discharge every capacitor on it rated 50 V or more, largest first, with your resistor tool (see safety_discharge_capacitor). On UV models do the same on the lamp's driver board.
steps.warn: On 120 V mains a power board's main capacitor can hold about 170 V DC; on 230 V mains about 340 V.

steps.text: Prove each one empty. Check your meter on a known source, measure DC volts across the capacitor (under 1 V), and check the meter on the known source again. Clip a jumper wire across the terminals of any large one while you work.
steps.warn: If a reading stays above 1 V, discharge again and measure again.

steps.text: Ionizer models: find the high-voltage module (a small sealed block with a thin wire running to needles, brushes or wires in the air stream). Leave it, its output wire and its emitters where they are: don't unplug, cut or lift them out. If it blocks another part, leave that part.
steps.warn: Don't touch the emitter points or the module's output wire. The module's output voltage is unknown and may be beyond your meter's range, so you cannot prove it empty. Winix warns that the high voltage inside its purifier may cause shock.

steps.text: Photograph the wiring and put a tape label on each plug before you unplug anything.
Unplug the fan motor's connector from the board, undo the screws holding the fan housing, and lift out the fan with its motor.
Undo the control board's screws and lift it out with its buttons. Then unplug and take the sensors: a particle (PM2.5) sensor box on auto models, and any odour or light sensor.
Separate the carbon stage: a carbon-coated pre-filter, a separate carbon filter or a tray of granules. Keep loose granules dry in a sealed bag.
Cut the mains cord off where it enters the case and keep it whole with its plug.

If the purifier came with a remote, take its button battery out and keep it away from children. Winix warns that a swallowed lithium button cell can cause severe internal burns and death in as little as 2 hours: get medical help at once if one is swallowed.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **HEPA filter.** Winix says its True HEPA filter catches 99.97% of particles down to 0.3 µm, including mould spores, microbes and smoke, and can't be washed (Winix 5500-2 manual). GermGuardian likewise says not to wash and reuse its combination filter (GermGuardian AC4825 manual). An unused spare is the prize. A spare may do the same job as the EPA's DIY cleaner, a box fan with a MERV 13 furnace filter. The EPA found these almost completely ineffective once the filter was dirty, and advises a 2012 or later box fan with a UL or ETL mark: it does not recommend older fans, and says they shouldn't run unattended or while you sleep (EPA DIY air cleaners). That page covers furnace filters, not HEPA panels, so seal the edges well and check the airflow. Use only an unused HEPA filter indoors.
- **Carbon.** Winix says its carbon filter reduces VOCs and household odours from cooking, pets and smoke, and can be washed without soap and must dry for 24 hours (Winix 5500-2 manual; Winix America 5500-2 manual). Don't put used carbon from an air filter into a drinking-water filter: you can't know what it has soaked up.
- **Fan and motor.** A quiet, low-power blower for ventilation, a dehydrator or a solder-fume extractor. Read the motor label. A motor marked for mains AC runs straight from mains; a brushless DC motor usually needs the board that drove it, so keep the two together.
- **UV-C lamp.** GermGuardian uses 5 W and 8 W UV-C bulbs (LB4000 and LB5000), says skin or eye damage can result from looking at the lit lamp, and says the lamp contains mercury (GermGuardian AC4825 manual). It needs its driver board to light. Only ever run it inside a closed housing that no light can escape from.
- **Sensors and board.** A particle sensor can become an air-quality monitor if you can find its pinout. The board's buttons, connectors and small parts are spares.
- **Cord.** A light mains lead.

## Testing what you got out

- **HEPA filter.** Hold it up to light: look for tears, holes and gaps at the frame. A clogged one is near useless (EPA DIY air cleaners).
- **Fan.** A mains motor: bench-test only through an RCD or GFCI, with the terminals covered and the blades guarded. A DC motor: keep bench tests at 30 V or less and within its label. A brushless one may not turn at all without its board.
- **UV-C lamp.** Don't test it in the open. Test it only back inside its own unit with every cover and shield on.

## Variations

- **GermGuardian AC4825 (UV-C).** 120 V. A combination filter with a pre-filter, charcoal and HEPA layers, and a UV-C bulb under a screwed metal shield. The UV light works with titanium dioxide (TiO2) to break down odours. GermGuardian gives an 8-hour average ozone level of 0.001 ppmv in a 30 m3 test chamber, and says the product meets a 0.050 ppmv 24-hour limit (GermGuardian AC4825 manual). If the lamp breaks, it points to the EPA's clean-up steps (EPA broken CFL).
- **Winix 5500-2 (PlasmaWave).** 120 V. A pre-filter, a washable carbon filter, a True HEPA filter and PlasmaWave, which Winix says makes hydroxyls and may chirp or buzz in use. It has odour and light sensors (Winix 5500-2 manual). Winix warns that the high voltage inside may cause electric shock, not to touch the interior with wet hands, and never to disassemble the unit yourself, and its remote holds a lithium button cell (Winix America 5500-2 manual).
- **Fulminare H13 (ionizer).** Its ionizer wires put out negative ions. The shell halves clip together, the fan is held by four screws and the board by two (iFixit Fulminare H13).
- Models with no UV, Ion or PlasmaWave marking may be just filters, fan, board and cord, but look inside before you assume it.

## What to leave

- **The ionizer and its high-voltage module.** A shock risk with no good reuse. The EPA notes that some units sold as air cleaners are ozone generators with an ionizer in the same case, and that ozone damages the lungs when inhaled (EPA ozone generators). Don't rebuild one into a room device.
- **A broken UV-C lamp:** clean it up as above, switch off any forced-air heating or cooling while you do, and keep it sealed in its jar (EPA broken CFL).
- **Used filters.** Keep them bagged and out of living space.
- The plastic shell, unless you need a small enclosure.
